paragraphs.heading: A ring of pressure around the pole
paragraphs.text: The Arctic oscillation, also called the Northern Annular Mode, is a weather pattern over the far north, above 55 degrees latitude. It counts as an important pattern of climate variability for the whole Northern Hemisphere. Its pressure changes form a ring, or annulus, centred on the pole. In the north, continents and big landmasses break that ring up, while the matching pattern around Antarctica, called the Southern Annular Mode, is almost a perfect circle.

paragraphs.heading: A seesaw with no clock
paragraphs.text: At heart it is a seesaw of sea-level air pressure. When pressure over the Arctic sits above or below normal, pressure in a band at about 37 to 45 degrees north tends to move the opposite way. The swing keeps no regular rhythm, flipping between positive and negative values on daily, monthly, seasonal and yearly scales. Edward Lorenz first spotted this seesaw, and David Thompson and John Michael Wallace gave it its name in 1998.

paragraphs.heading: The positive phase
paragraphs.text: The AO index, a number built from surface air pressure patterns, is linked to how far Arctic air pushes into the middle latitudes. When the index is positive, pressure over the polar region is high. That helps the jet stream of the middle latitudes blow hard and steadily from west to east, which keeps the coldest air shut in near the pole. Much of the United States east of the Rockies then stays warmer than normal, while Greenland and Newfoundland turn colder. Ocean storms also shift north, bringing wetter weather to Alaska, Scotland and Scandinavia and drier weather to the western United States and the Mediterranean.

paragraphs.heading: The negative phase
paragraphs.text: When the index is negative, the polar region tends to have low pressure, the west-to-east winds weaken, and frigid air moves more freely into the middle latitudes. Weather in this phase is broadly the reverse of the positive one. February 2010 shows what that can look like. That month the index fell to about −4.266, its lowest monthly value since 1950, and three historic snowstorms struck the mid-Atlantic United States. Baltimore got 25 inches of snow on February 5–6, and New York City got 20.9 inches on February 25–26.

paragraphs.heading: Europe in the deep freeze
paragraphs.text: A negative phase was also blamed for harsh cold in western Europe during the first three weeks of one December. Two major snowstorms, ice and bitter temperatures caused chaos across much of the region. A stubborn ridge of high pressure near Greenland, known as a blocking system, let Arctic air slide south into Europe. North America was hit too, with a large snowstorm and frigid temperatures in the US Midwest from December 10 to 13.

paragraphs.heading: Measuring and forecasting it
paragraphs.text: The index is worked out from daily or monthly anomalies in the height of the 1000 hPa pressure level, between 20 and 90 degrees north. These are compared against the standard shape of the pattern, taken from 1979–2000 data, and the result is then scaled. Averaged over 60 days, the index has leaned toward its positive phase since the 1970s, though over the last decade it has drifted back toward neutral. Short-range forecasts do well: seven-day forecasts from the Global Forecast System match what actually happens with a correlation of about 0.9.
